claims.text: Chemical short-range order suppresses lattice thermal conductivity in concentrated refractory high-entropy alloys between 300 K and 1000 K.
The thermal-conductivity suppression is caused by diffuse antiphase boundaries acting as strong phonon-scattering centers.
Above 1500 K, thermal entropy disrupts SRO and reduces its transport effect.
Loss of SRO at high temperature restores lattice transport toward that of a random solid solution.
A random-solid-solution MoNbTaW or W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf alloy has a homogeneous atomic distribution, negligible SRO, and high lattice distortion.
Equilibration or annealing at 800 K can induce SRO in MoNbTaW.
Annealing at 800 K for 24 hours followed by quenching will produce and preserve SRO without phase separation or precipitation.
The order-disorder transition temperature of W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf is near its irradiation temperature while the alloy remains single-phase BCC.
DAPBs form at interfaces between locally ordered clusters and the random matrix and create a periodic or semiperiodic potential variation.
The energy required to break local chemical order during phonon propagation enhances phonon scattering.
Random-solute phonon scattering is isotropic, whereas SRO supplies a correlation length that resonates with selected phonon wavelengths.
At high temperature, the entropic term overcomes the ordering energy and drives the SRO parameter toward zero.
The SRO sample will have 15–25% lower lattice thermal conductivity than the RSS sample from 300 K to 1000 K.
A fully random solid solution can be obtained by quenching from above the order-disorder transition or by high-energy ball milling followed by low-temperature annealing.
Secondary phases such as Laves phases or Cr-V precipitates independently scatter phonons and confound the SRO effect.
W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf develops precipitation at high irradiation doses or temperatures.
Grain boundaries in sputtered films with grain sizes below 50 nm may dominate phonon scattering and mask the SRO effect.
Specific-heat measurements can isolate the lattice contribution from the measured total thermal conductivity.

contradictions.description: The stated measurement conditions end at 1500 K, while the hypothesis makes a prediction for temperatures above 1500 K and the experimental design extends to 1600 K.

The quantitative suppression prediction is limited to 300–1000 K, but the falsification rule requires lower conductivity at every temperature below 1500 K, extending the claim into the otherwise unspecified 1000–1500 K interval.
